items.summaryKo: And some we're still ambivalent about. In the first part of this series, Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian and critic Aruna D'Souza discussed the pavilions they loved at the 61st Venice Biennale, running through November 22, and even made a provocative argument in favor of national pavilions. In this second and final installment, they take their gloves off to tear apart the pavilions they didn't like and argue about the ones they're split on. Brace yourself; it's going to get heated. An excerpt from Alexis Pauline Gumbs’s book on the late painter, plus reviews of new titles by Sophie Lewis and Dana Mashoian Walrath. Reading through Undrowned a few years ago, I marveled at poet and scholar Alexis Pauline Gumbs’s ability to see a confluence of marine mammal life and Black feminist thought that others couldn’t. (Plus, as a child of the Finding Nemo era, I suspected she’d cracked open a new way to frame our collective fascination with the sea.) So. when I heard that she was writing a book about the late artist Alma Thomas, I couldn’t wait to see how she applied her signature tenderness, sorely lacking in much of mainstream criticism, to the beloved paintings. When Gumbs looks at Thomas’s canvases, she sees braids, heirloom corn, and the root system of history. In an exquisite excerpt from Primary: After and With Alma Thomas , Gumbs draws on the writing of historian Richard J. Powell to reframe Thomas’s “color fields. as cornrows,” blending poetry and biography to theorize what grounds much of Black diasporic visual culture: the art of sistering. In another nod to marine life, author Sophie Lewis’s Femmephilia: Love Letters to Trans Mermaids, Queer Mothers, and Marilyn Monroe tackles the politics and erotic power of femme aesthetics, still rejected and ridiculed even in some contemporary feminist circles. Critic Eileen G’Sell, ever preoccupied with questions of glamour, authenticity, and adornment, reviews the book below. Read on for Noah Fischer’s candid reflec.

items.titleOriginal: From the Bronx to the Lower East Side, New York’s museum building boom continues
items.summaryKo: Several institutional construction projects have already opened this year, with more in the pipeline A render of the Grand Concourse entrance of The Bronx Museum’s South Wing, which aims to better connect to the community and shows a sloped, geometric roof and a glass façade that works with the adjacent origami-like building This year has already seen the completion of several long-awaited institutional building projects in New York, from Harlem to the Bowery, but some ambitious developments are. still on the horizon as the city’s cultural landscape continues to evolve. Canyon , a forthcoming 40,000-sq.-ft contemporary art space on the Lower East Side, is tentatively due to open in the new year. The institution was founded by the philanthropist and art collector Robert Rosenkranz and is spearheaded by Joe Thompson, the founding director of the Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, who spent more than three decades building that museum into a leading venue for large-scale art. Thompson describes Canyon as “neither a conventional museum nor a kunsthalle ”, but a “space for art that invites you to stay a while”. The New York-based firm New Affiliates Architecture spearheaded the $40m project, redesigning a previously commercial space. It will feature 18,000 sq. ft of galleries, a 60ft-tall skylit atrium, a café, a full-service restaurant and bar, and will be open late. items.titleOriginal: Beer With a Painter: Barbara Takenaga
items.summaryKo: The Japanese-American artist talks about her place as a paint dot in the universe and embracing disruption in her canvases. With tiny filaments of paint that repeat into monumental surfaces, Barbara Takenaga’s paintings thrill and seduce but do not rest in their elegance. They suggest menacing storms, disintegrating shapes, unknowable black holes, awkward interactions, and bodily processes. Takenaga describes herself as a process painter, and her work requires a stunning amount of labor. But it isn’t perfection that she is after: She. values the fourth-wall breaks that disrupt illusions and the elements that throw off purist systems. As a person, she has a wry sense of humor and a humility that connects to the humanity and interruptions visible in her work. One side of Takenaga’s Manhattan studio is loaded with all of her tools — careful stacks of acrylic paint jars, cups, baskets of small brushes, and books and reproductions posted on the wall — while the other side is completely open, its wood. floors leading to windows overlooking the Flatiron District, lined with potted plants soaking up the light. In some ways, it feels like an echo of her paintings’ composition, with their deep space, dramatic horizon lines, patterns that coalesce into voids, and shapes that mass into tornado-like forms.
